newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Kasai is diamond-rich centre of opposition.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Kasai is diamond-rich centre of opposition.

text.p: The mining capital of Mbuji-Mayi and the surrounding Kasai region of central Zaire is a diamond-rich land of opposition to President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Kasai even uses different money to defy the ailing president and is a crucial test of support for the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).

Mining sources in the town said the main force of AFDL rebels entered Mbuji-Mayi on Saturday morning. Earlier, government troops had looted vehicles and shops before fleeing towards the town of Kananga, 100 km (62 miles) to the west.
Mbuji-Mayi is the homeland of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, whose offer to rebels of six ministry posts in his new government was rebuffed.

But support for Tshisekedi is strong in Kasai, where his Baluba people in 1993 heeded his call to boycott new bank notes introduced by Mobutu. The old notes are still in use and as a side effect defeat hyperinflation rampant everywhere else.
AFDL leader Laurent Kabila's origins also lie with the Baluba, but in a subgroup from neighbouring mineral-rich Shaba.
Kasai residents still remember how hundreds of thousands of Kasaians were expelled from Shaba during ethnic violence in the early 1990s.

The rebel force is dominated by ethnic Tutsis, some of them Zairean Banyamulenge Tutsis and others said by intelligence sources to be members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army. The Rwandan government denies any involvement with the rebels.
Demobilised Ugandan troops, hired on contract, are also part of the rebel force. Kabila is a Zairean non-Tutsi from Shaba and his field commanders are a mixture of Zaireans and foreigners.
Perceived by Mobutu largely as an opposition bastion during his 32 years of rule, Kasai has suffered even more than the rest of the dilapidated country from central government neglect.
Kasaians have joined together in self-help organisations to take over the role of the absent state -- repairing roads and even planning an ambitious $13 million hydro-electric dam.
Subsistence farmers populate most of the area, which hides pockets of very significant diamond wealth.

Societe Miniere de Bakwanga (MIBA) mines produce most of the world's small industrial diamonds and have been a huge source of government revenue since the collapse of copper and cobalt mining to the southwest.
Mining of both industrial and gem stones has helped make Mbuji-Mayi a centre for fortune hunters. Bottles of champagne can often be seen next to tins of sardines in its markets.

Predictions that Mbuji-Mayi is being dug out have turned the western Kasai town of Tshikapa into a new focus of the diamond trade, both in its own right and as a staging post for stones smuggled from neighbouring Angola.

At independence from Belgium in 1960 South Kasai joined Shaba's ill-fated bid to secede from the rest of the country, then known as the Congo, but since then Kasaians have focused more on gaining political power in Kinshasa than breaking away.
Murdered independence prime minister and national hero Patrice Lumumba's origins lay in Kasai, among a minority tribe rather than the main Baluba ethnic group.
Almost all Zairean politicians, including Tshisekedi, Kabila and Mobutu, have said they stood for his nationalistic ideals.
